overview.body:
**Susanō** (*susanoo*) — Storms, Sea, Chaos · Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god — belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Storms, Sea, Chaos". The name means "Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god"[^1].

**Susanō** belongs to the Japanese tradition, where it is associated with storms, sea, chaos.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Susanō** and serves its temple at [susanoo.com](https://punicodex.com/susanoo/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *susanoo* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^2].

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.
Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Japanese characters as **須佐之男命**. Etymologically it means "Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god"[^1].

From Old Japanese susanowo, 'swift impetuous male'; brother of Amaterasu, expelled from the high plain of heaven for his violence.

The ASCII form *susanoo* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Susanō** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **s** → **S** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **o** → **ō** — Macron: long vowel
- **o** → **o** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **susanoo.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.
Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/susanoo/** — Japanese Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **S** — Initial character of the restored form Susanō.
- **usanō** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Japanese tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'SUSANOO' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Japanese** — Susanō, the restored Unicode form of the name

Susanō is Tier 1 because the Japanese form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

original-script.body: The name is written in Japanese characters as **須佐之男命**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *susanoo* and the PuniCodex restoration **Susanō** are measured: the restoration preserves its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

mythology.body:
The stories of **Susanō** circulate within the Japanese corpus, where the figure embodies storms, sea, chaos.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Susanō is attested in the canonical Japanese sources as a figure associated with storms, sea, chaos.[^1]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Swift impetuous male deity; the Shinto storm god" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Susanō** is the Shinto storm god, brother of Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi. The *Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki* recount his quarrel with Amaterasu: after rampaging through her heavenly fields, she withdraws into a cave and plunges the world into darkness.[^1] Susanō later atones by slaying the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi at Izumo and recovering the sword Kusanagi, one of the imperial regalia.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), Translated by W. G. Aston (excerpts), 720.

syncretism.body:
Susanō appears within the Japanese tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Japanese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[fujin|Fūjin]], [[hokkaido|Hokkaidō]], [[honshu|Honshū]], [[jizo|Jizō]], [[kobe|Kōbe]], and [[kyoto|Kyōto]].

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

cultural-legacy.body: Susanō continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Japanese tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] Susanō remains central to Izumo Taisha and to Japanese concepts of unruly divine power that can be redirected toward protection.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

meditation.body: Susanō embodies storms, sea, chaos in the Japanese imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), Translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, 712.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The **Kojiki** recounts Susanō's expulsion from Takamagahara after his rampage through Amaterasu's rice fields, followed by his descent to Izumo and slaying of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi.[^1] The **Nihon Shoki** offers variant accounts that emphasize his stormy character and his gift of the **Kusanagi sword** to Amaterasu.[^2]

Together these chronicles make Susanō the paradigmatic exiled kami whose violence ultimately produces order.

sources.citation: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters), 712.
Nihon Shoki (Chronicles of Japan), 720.

shinto-sources.body:
The **Izumo Fudoki** and shrine rituals (*norito*) preserve Susanō's local cult at the **Grand Shrine of Izumo**, where he is honoured as ruler of the unseen world (*ne-no-kuni*).[^1] Seasonal festivals and the **Kamiari-mōde** reflect his role as mediator between the visible and invisible realms.[^2]

Susanō is thus as much a Shinto land-god as a storm-god.

sources.citation: Fudoki (Records of Wind and Earth), Izumo Fudoki.
Shinto (Kojiki, Nihon Shoki, shrine rituals, and folk practice).

buddhist-japanese.body:
In medieval Japan Susanō was syncretised with **Gozu Tennō**, a wrathful Buddhist protector who subdues plague demons.[^1] The **Tendai** and **Shugendō** traditions recast his storm-power as a compassionate ferocity that destroys obstacles to enlightenment.[^2]

This *shinbutsu-shūgō* blending made Susanō a boundary-crossing figure who could be worshipped in both shrine and temple.
